place-context.text: Mound City’s reported construction sequence, a Hopeton wall trench, Hopewell Mound Group’s historical plan and contemporary Myaamia statements locate different kinds of evidence. A modern property-center point or shared earthwork form does not establish a direct route, one building date or one state.

coordination.text: Dispersed households could gather at shared ceremonial places; a large enclosure need not be a permanently inhabited town.

evidence-limits.text: Survey plans, nonlocal materials, excavation and restoration each answer different questions.

name: Ohio Hopewell: gathering places and distant materials
place: Ohio River tributaries; locator at Mound City Group, Ohio, United States
geographicPrecision: One ceremonial site within a wider network; neither a tribal capital nor an imperial border.

interval.label: Selected Ohio ceremonial networks, c. 1–400 CE
interval.note: NPS focus for these earthworks. Hopewell is an archaeological network label; the bounds do not date the existence of every related community.

question: How could dispersed communities create shared monumental places?
summary: People provisioned households, built ceremonial structures, moved selected soils and returned to shared places. Historical plans, a restored landscape, one dated Hopeton wall investigation and named contemporary Myaamia accounts explain different parts of that work and its continuing significance.

sections.title: Shared places and everyday provision
sections.text: In the Ohio tributary valleys, Indigenous communities made gathering places whose shapes still organize the landscape. The atlas follows selected works between 1 and 400 CE; Hopewell is an archaeological label for linked practices among different groups. It does not supply the builders’ own collective name. Monumental work could bring people together without requiring everyone to live permanently inside one enclosure. Shared construction and repeated meetings are part of the explanation for how dispersed communities made public places.

citations.locator: History & Culture: 1–400 CE focus and broad network

sections.title: Food work sustained other work
sections.text: Building depended on ordinary ways of sustaining life. The NPS account describes hunting, fishing and gathering alongside cultivated annual plants. Sunflower, squash and goosefoot were among the crops grown in Ohio before maize and beans became established later. Fields near homes, produced and gathered foods and knowledge of local environments supported households as well as other activities. The account connects household food work with the energy needed to build and use shared places.

citations.locator: Introductory paragraphs before Eastern Agricultural Complex Plants

sections.title: Building, dismantling and adding earth
sections.text: At Mound City, a mound could follow a ceremonial building. Builders erected poles and bark over a plastered clay floor, and fires burned in clay basins. Some ceremonies honored the dead. The building was later deliberately dismantled before earth was added. Alternating deposits of clay and sand show planned material work. NPS suggests mound building may have continued through several gatherings; the layers do not count the meetings or identify a single commander.

sections.title: A wall preserves a particular sequence
sections.text: Hopeton provides another construction example. The NPS report of investigations in 2001–02 describes trenches across enclosure walls. Builders first stripped topsoil and then brought in other soils in layers. A burned-log sample led the report to place the beginning of one sampled wall around 300 CE. The work therefore involved choosing, moving and placing material. That reported estimate belongs to a particular wall investigation, rather than dating every enclosure or every community.

citations.locator: Ongoing Research: 2001–02 trenches, soil layers and burned-log estimate

sections.title: Materials, skill and continuing responsibility
sections.text: Copper, mica, shell and obsidian connected Ohio ceremonial objects with distant material sources. Their presence establishes movement, while leaving several possible chains of exchange and travel. Modern knowledge also includes people who care for these places. Writing in the Miami Tribe’s 2023 newspaper, Chief Douglas Lankford encouraged Myaamia people to visit the earthworks respectfully within their homelands. Logan York, identified there as the Tribe’s Historic Preservation Officer, described the builders’ abilities and pride in their recognition. These are named contemporary perspectives on responsibility and ancestral achievement.

deeperReading.title: A plan is a dated act of recording
deeperReading.text: The winter photograph and North Fork Works plan show different sites. The photograph records restored Mound City; the 1848 survey records Hopewell Mound Group. The latter includes a large enclosure, a smaller square and internal forms, alongside the nineteenth-century landscape. Its geometry is useful evidence, but its title and publication date belong to later observers. The name Hopewell came from a landowner. NPS’s account follows changing investigations, from earlier defensive readings to mapping and later magnetometry; these interpretations should remain distinguishable.

citations.locator: New to Science; Archeological Expeditions; 1848 North Fork Works illustration

deeperReading.title: Compare records without flattening time
deeperReading.text: The separate 1848 Mound City plate supports a same-site comparison with the winter photograph. It shows the enclosure beside the Scioto River and a canal, with another circular work farther down the sheet. The canal belongs to the surveyors’ landscape, not the ancient building episode. The modern visitor map adds trails, parking and interpretation. Neither document is a single ancient phase. At Hopeton, later plowing and quarrying changed what remained above ground, while survey and excavation answer different spatial questions.

citations.locator: Squier & Davis, c.1848 illustration; Site Map & Trail Map

deeperReading.title: Names and period boundaries need attribution
deeperReading.text: The period labels have different scopes. Newark Earthworks Center’s FAQ places its archaeological culture around 100 BCE–400 CE; York’s 2023 article describes a wider Hopewell religious movement around 100 BCE–500 CE. The selected NPS inquiry remains 1–400 CE. None of these frames ends Indigenous presence or makes all structures contemporary. The Myaamia statements concern return and recognition in 2023, rather than preserving transcripts of ancient ceremonies.

evidenceReading.title: A plan, a sampled wall and contemporary voices
evidenceReading.introduction: These supplied passages are editorial paraphrases. Spatial records, excavation results and named modern statements answer different questions; none replaces the others.

items.label: The North Fork Works plan and winter photograph record different sites
items.text: The 1848 North Fork Works plan records Hopewell Mound Group. The 2013 winter photograph shows restored Mound City. NPS describes documentary research and surviving bases behind the visible Mound City restorations.
items.interpretation: Compare what kinds of evidence the images supply, rather than overlaying them as matching views. A historical plan, a modern restoration and a photograph each have their own dates. Neither records every ancient construction episode or ceremony.

citations.locator: Introduction; A National Park is Born

items.label: One trench supplies a relative order and a reported date
items.text: The NPS project account, updated 20 July 2020, reports investigations carried out in 2001–02. Trenches crossing Hopeton’s square enclosure revealed topsoil removal followed by added soil layers. It associates a burned-log result in one trench with initial construction of one wall around 300 CE.
items.interpretation: Stratigraphy supports an order of operations. The reported wood date constrains one investigation; its rounded estimate is not a calibrated probability interval supplied here. It cannot make all walls simultaneous. Nor does a material sequence identify the organization that recruited every worker.

citations.locator: Ongoing Research, paragraph beginning Excavations during 2001 and 2002 and following paragraph

items.label: Myaamia authors address responsibility and recognition
items.text: Chief Douglas Lankford’s 2023 report encourages respectful visits to the earthworks within Myaamia homelands. Logan York’s article in the same issue describes ancestral achievement and his participation in World Heritage recognition.
items.interpretation: These are attributed contemporary perspectives published by the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma. They support an account of living relationships with these places; they are not transcripts of ancient beliefs, archaeological proof of one direct lineage or statements for all Native peoples.

citations.locator: The Chief Report, p. 3A, Hopewell paragraphs; Logan York, p. 5A

familyActivity.title: Follow the work before the mound
steps: Read the supplied source capsule together. Draw three boxes and give each reported stage a work verb.
Choose two different materials in the capsule. Explain where each belongs in the sequence, without inventing a building size or a thickness for a layer.
Make one claim about how people prepared a shared place. Name the supplied detail supporting it, then explain what further evidence would be needed to count the gatherings.
If you compare the two older images, say their site names first: the winter photograph is Mound City; the North Fork Works plan is Hopewell Mound Group. They are not matching views of one place.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase of NPS Careful Construction: at Mound City, builders erected a poles-and-bark ceremonial building with a plastered clay floor. The building was deliberately dismantled before earthen mound additions. NPS reports layers and suggests building may have happened through repeated gatherings. Preparing a floor, dismantling and moving material are supported kinds of work; the capsule gives neither a counted schedule nor an identified commander. The separate historical plan is a later spatial record, not a picture of those operations.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author review; not independent historian or community approval
review.scope: Work and gathering account, attributed wider context, three evidence readings, supplied family source capsule and separately sourced Mound City plan. Complete original identity, interval, claims, prior dimensions and original object order retained.
limitations: NPS construction descriptions and its 2001–02 Hopeton project account were consulted, not the original field notebooks or raw radiocarbon calibration tables. Around 300 CE belongs to one reported sampled-wall investigation; wood/sample age and all-site construction must not be conflated.

Broader religious-movement and archaeological-culture conventions differ across York and Newark Earthworks Center. They remain attributed, while the original complete 1–400 CE case is unchanged. No exact Mound City phase dates, work-party counts, labor calendar or centralized state reconstructed.

Contemporary 2023 Myaamia authors represent named perspectives on recognition, homelands and respect. Their statements are outside ancient phases and do not establish identical ancient beliefs or a lineage proved by artifacts. No protected or unrelated community material reproduced.

Both inherited image pixels and two selected plan/map reproductions were actually inspected. The old NPS gallery source retains its 27 October asset-specific consultation; this renewal exposed only generic usage text. No current remote-byte parity or fresh asset-specific 2013 metadata verification claimed. Small historical scans stay small. The modern visitor map was inspected in research only; it is not the adopted 1848 survey.

The Smithsonian catalogue was consulted as metadata, not the full book. The full UNESCO nomination and Benjamin Barnes essay were unavailable at the selected access scope and not read. Eastern Shawnee full-page and large Absentee Shawnee newsletter access gaps remain documented.
Independent historian/community review, actual adult/family use, human screen-reader behavior, physical devices and physical print quality remain open.
